info.articulations: Both parietal bones at the coronal suture, plus the sphenoid, ethmoid, nasal, lacrimal, zygomatic and maxillary bones.
info.landmarks: Supraorbital margin and supraorbital foramen or notch, glabella, superciliary arches, zygomatic process, and the frontal sinus.
info.fact: A metopic suture that fails to close persists in the adult midline and can be mistaken for a fracture on radiographs.

info.articulations: The opposite parietal at the sagittal suture, the frontal, occipital, temporal and the greater wing of the sphenoid.
info.landmarks: Parietal eminence, superior and inferior temporal lines, parietal foramen, and internal grooves for the middle meningeal vessels.
info.fact: At the pterion the parietal meets the frontal, temporal and sphenoid over the middle meningeal artery, a dangerously thin spot.

info.articulations: The parietal, occipital, sphenoid and zygomatic bones, and the mandible at the temporomandibular joint.
info.landmarks: External acoustic meatus, mastoid and styloid processes, zygomatic process, mandibular fossa, carotid canal, and stylomastoid foramen.
info.fact: Its petrous part houses the inner ear, and the facial nerve leaves through the stylomastoid foramen just behind the styloid process.

info.articulations: Both parietal bones at the lambdoid suture, both temporal bones, the sphenoid, and the atlas at the occipital condyles.
info.landmarks: Foramen magnum, occipital condyles, hypoglossal canal, external occipital protuberance, and the internal grooves for the dural venous sinuses.
info.fact: The condyles form the atlanto-occipital joints, the yes joint of nodding, while the foramen magnum transmits the medulla.

info.articulations: The frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, ethmoid, vomer, zygomatic, palatine and maxillary bones, twelve bones in all.
info.landmarks: Sella turcica and hypophyseal fossa, greater and lesser wings, optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum, pterygoid processes.
info.fact: Shaped like a butterfly, it is the keystone of the cranial base and cradles the pituitary gland in its sella turcica.

info.articulations: The frontal and sphenoid above, and the nasal, lacrimal, maxillary, palatine, inferior conchal bones and vomer of the face.
info.landmarks: Cribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate, superior and middle nasal conchae, and the ethmoidal air cells.
info.fact: A fractured cribriform plate can tear the olfactory nerves and leak cerebrospinal fluid from the nose, causing anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea.

info.articulations: The opposite maxilla, plus the frontal, ethmoid, nasal, lacrimal, zygomatic, palatine, inferior nasal concha and vomer.
info.landmarks: Infraorbital foramen, alveolar process, frontal, zygomatic and palatine processes, anterior nasal spine, and the maxillary sinus.
info.fact: The maxillary sinus drains upward into the middle meatus, so it clears poorly when upright and is the commonest site of sinusitis.

info.articulations: The frontal bone, the greater wing of the sphenoid, the temporal bone at the zygomatic arch, and the maxilla.
info.landmarks: Temporal process forming the zygomatic arch, frontal process, orbital surface, and the zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal foramina.
info.fact: The cheekbone is often broken in facial trauma, typically as a tripod fracture separating it from the frontal, temporal and maxillary attachments.

info.articulations: The frontal bone above, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid behind, the opposite nasal bone, and the maxilla laterally.
info.landmarks: Internasal suture, the nasion at its junction with the frontal bone, nasal foramen, and the free inferior border for the nasal cartilages.
info.fact: The nasal bone is the most frequently fractured bone of the face, since only its upper part is bone and the rest cartilage.

info.articulations: The frontal bone above, the ethmoid behind, the maxilla in front, and the inferior nasal concha below.
info.landmarks: Lacrimal groove or fossa for the lacrimal sac, posterior lacrimal crest, and the lacrimal hamulus completing the nasolacrimal canal.
info.fact: It is the smallest and most fragile bone of the face, and its groove carries tears down into the inferior meatus of the nose.

info.articulations: The opposite palatine bone, the maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, inferior nasal concha and vomer.
info.landmarks: Horizontal and perpendicular plates, pyramidal process, orbital and sphenoidal processes, and the greater and lesser palatine foramina.
info.fact: Failure of the horizontal plates and palatine processes to fuse in the midline produces cleft palate.

info.articulations: The ethmoid, maxilla, lacrimal bone and palatine bone of the same side of the lateral nasal wall.
info.landmarks: Lacrimal, maxillary and ethmoidal processes, and the curved shelf overhanging the inferior meatus.
info.fact: It is the only concha that is a separate bone, since the superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid.

info.articulations: The sphenoid and ethmoid above, both maxillae and both palatine bones below, and the septal cartilage in front.
info.landmarks: Alae that grip the sphenoid rostrum, the thin vertical plate, and the free posterior border separating the choanae.
info.fact: Vomer is Latin for ploughshare, which its shape resembles; it forms the posteroinferior nasal septum and is often deviated.

info.articulations: Only the two temporal bones, at the temporomandibular joints between its condyles and the mandibular fossae.
info.landmarks: Body, ramus and angle, condylar and coronoid processes, mental foramen, mandibular foramen with its lingula, and the mylohyoid line.
info.fact: It is the only mobile bone of the skull, and the temporomandibular joint is the skull's only synovial joint.

info.articulations: It articulates with no other bone, being slung from the styloid processes of the temporal bones by the stylohyoid ligaments.
info.landmarks: Body, paired greater horns and paired lesser horns, giving attachment to the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles.
info.fact: The only bone in the body with no bony articulation; a fractured hyoid strongly suggests manual strangulation.

info.articulations: The occipital condyles above at the atlanto-occipital joints, and the axis below at the lateral and median atlanto-axial joints.
info.landmarks: Anterior and posterior arches with their tubercles, lateral masses, transverse foramina, facet for the dens, and the groove for the vertebral artery.
info.fact: The atlas has no body and no spinous process; it carries the skull and forms the yes joint of nodding.

info.articulations: The atlas above at the median and lateral atlanto-axial joints, and C3 below by an intervertebral disc and facet joints.
info.landmarks: Dens or odontoid process, superior articular facets on the body, strong bifid spinous process, and transverse foramina.
info.fact: The dens is the pivot for the no movement of head rotation; fracture of its pars interarticularis is the hangman's fracture.

info.articulations: C2 above and C4 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Small broad body with uncinate processes, bifid spinous process, transverse foramen, and anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process.
info.fact: C3 is the first typical cervical vertebra, and the hyoid bone lies at this level in the neck.

info.articulations: C3 above and C5 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Uncinate processes on the body, bifid spinous process, transverse foramen for the vertebral artery, and grooved transverse process for the spinal nerve.
info.fact: The common carotid artery divides at about the C4 level, at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.

info.articulations: C4 above and C6 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Uncinate processes, bifid spinous process, transverse foramen, and superior articular facets facing backward and upward.
info.fact: Remember that C3, C4 and C5 keep the diaphragm alive, since these roots form the phrenic nerve.

info.articulations: C5 above and C7 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Prominent anterior tubercle of the transverse process, the carotid tubercle, plus transverse foramen, uncinate processes and a bifid spinous process.
info.fact: The carotid artery can be compressed against the carotid tubercle of C6, the level where the larynx becomes trachea and pharynx becomes oesophagus.

info.articulations: C6 above and T1 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Long non-bifid spinous process, small transverse foramen, prominent posterior tubercle, and uncinate processes on the body.
info.fact: Called the vertebra prominens for its long single-tipped spine; its transverse foramen transmits small veins, not the vertebral artery.

info.articulations: C7 above and T2 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the first and second ribs.
info.landmarks: Full costal facet for rib one with an inferior demifacet for rib two, long horizontal spinous process, and transverse costal facets.
info.fact: T1 is atypical because it carries a complete costal facet for rib one, and its body resembles a cervical vertebra with uncinate processes.

info.articulations: T1 above and T3 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the second and third ribs.
info.landmarks: Superior and inferior costal demifacets, transverse process costal facets, heart-shaped body, and a long downward-sloping spinous process.
info.fact: The jugular notch of the manubrium lies at about the T2 to T3 level, a useful surface landmark for counting down.

info.articulations: T2 above and T4 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the third and fourth ribs.
info.landmarks: Paired superior and inferior costal demifacets, costal facets on the transverse processes, and a long overlapping spinous process.
info.fact: The medial end of the spine of the scapula lies at the T3 level, a handy surface landmark on the back.

info.articulations: T3 above and T5 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the fourth and fifth ribs.
info.landmarks: Superior and inferior costal demifacets, transverse costal facets, heart-shaped body, and an obliquely downward spinous process.
info.fact: The sternal angle lies at the T4 to T5 disc, where the trachea divides and the arch of the aorta begins and ends.

info.articulations: T4 above and T6 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the fifth and sixth ribs.
info.landmarks: Superior and inferior costal demifacets, costal facets on the transverse processes, and a long steeply sloping spinous process.
info.fact: Mid-thoracic spines slope so steeply that the tip of the T5 spinous process lies opposite the body of the vertebra below.

info.articulations: T5 above and T7 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the sixth and seventh ribs.
info.landmarks: Heart-shaped body with superior and inferior costal demifacets, transverse costal facets, and a long overlapping spinous process.
info.fact: T6 is a textbook typical thoracic vertebra, with two costal demifacets each side and near-circular vertebral foramen.

info.articulations: T6 above and T8 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the seventh and eighth ribs.
info.landmarks: Superior and inferior costal demifacets, costal facets on the transverse processes, and the longest, most steeply angled spinous process.
info.fact: The inferior angle of the scapula lies at the T7 spinous process when the arms hang at the sides.

info.articulations: T7 above and T9 below by discs and facet joints, and with the heads of the eighth and ninth ribs.
info.landmarks: Superior and inferior costal demifacets, transverse process costal facets, and a long downward-directed spinous process.
info.fact: The caval opening of the diaphragm lies at the T8 level, transmitting the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve.

info.articulations: T8 above and T10 below by discs and facet joints, and with the head of the ninth rib and often the tenth.
info.landmarks: Superior costal demifacets, frequently absent inferior demifacets, transverse costal facets, and a long sloping spinous process.
info.fact: The xiphisternal joint lies at about the T9 level, and T9 often lacks inferior demifacets, making it atypical.

info.articulations: T9 above and T11 below by discs and facet joints, and with the head of the tenth rib.
info.landmarks: A single complete costal facet on each side of the body, costal facets on the transverse processes, and a shorter spinous process.
info.fact: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm lies at T10, transmitting the oesophagus and the vagal trunks.

info.articulations: T10 above and T12 below by discs and facet joints, and with the head of the eleventh rib.
info.landmarks: A single large complete costal facet on each side, transverse processes without costal facets, and a short triangular spinous process.
info.fact: T11 is atypical: its transverse processes bear no costal facets because rib eleven is a floating rib with no tubercle joint.

info.articulations: T11 above and L1 below by discs and facet joints, and with the head of the twelfth rib.
info.landmarks: Single complete costal facet each side, no transverse costal facets, short spinous process, and lumbar-type inferior articular facets.
info.fact: T12 is the transition vertebra, its inferior facets facing laterally like a lumbar vertebra; the aortic hiatus lies at this level.

info.articulations: T12 above and L2 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Large kidney-shaped body, hatchet-shaped spinous process, transverse costal processes, and mammillary and accessory processes.
info.fact: The spinal cord ends as the conus medullaris at about the L1 to L2 level, and the transpyloric plane crosses L1.

info.articulations: L1 above and L3 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Kidney-shaped body, triangular vertebral foramen, blunt spinous process, transverse process, and mammillary and accessory processes.
info.fact: Because the conus medullaris can end as low as L2, lumbar puncture is performed at L3 to L4 or below.

info.articulations: L2 above and L4 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Broad body, short sturdy spinous process, long transverse processes, superior articular facets facing medially, and the pars interarticularis.
info.fact: The umbilicus lies at about the L3 to L4 level in a person of average build.

info.articulations: L3 above and L5 below, each by an intervertebral disc and a pair of zygapophysial facet joints.
info.landmarks: Kidney-shaped body, hatchet-shaped spinous process, transverse processes, mammillary and accessory processes, and medially facing superior facets.
info.fact: The supracristal line joining the iliac crests crosses the L4 spine, guiding lumbar puncture; the aorta divides at this level.

info.articulations: L4 above by a disc and facet joints, and the sacrum below at the lumbosacral joint.
info.landmarks: The deepest body, taller in front than behind, massive transverse processes reaching the pedicles, and a small blunt spinous process.
info.fact: L5 is the largest vertebra and its wedge-shaped body forms the lumbosacral angle; spondylolisthesis occurs most often here.

info.articulations: L5 above at the lumbosacral joint, both hip bones at the sacroiliac joints, and the coccyx below.
info.landmarks: Sacral promontory, alae, anterior and posterior sacral foramina, median sacral crest, sacral canal, sacral hiatus, and auricular surface.
info.fact: Five fused vertebrae; the sacral hiatus at its lower end is the entry point for caudal epidural anaesthesia.

info.articulations: Body of T1 by a single facet on its head, the transverse process of T1 at its tubercle, and the manubrium through its costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Single facet on the head, scalene tubercle on the superior surface, and the grooves for the subclavian vein in front and artery behind.
info.fact: The shortest, broadest and most sharply curved rib; the subclavian vessels and lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross its flat top.

info.articulations: Bodies of T1 and T2 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T2 at its tubercle, and the sternum through its costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, tubercle, angle close to the tubercle, and the tuberosity for serratus anterior on its outer surface.
info.fact: Its cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle, the palpable landmark students use to start counting ribs downward.

info.articulations: Bodies of T2 and T3 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T3 at its tubercle, and the sternal body through its own costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Head with two facets, neck, tubercle with articular and non-articular parts, angle, and the costal groove on the inner lower border.
info.fact: The first fully typical rib, its costal groove shelters the intercostal vein, artery and nerve stacked in that order from above down.

info.articulations: Bodies of T3 and T4 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T4 at its tubercle, and the sternal body through its own costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle, and costal groove sheltering the intercostal neurovascular bundle.
info.fact: A typical true rib; in men the nipple usually overlies the fourth intercostal space, just below this rib.

info.articulations: Bodies of T4 and T5 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T5 at its tubercle, and the sternal body through its own costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle, and the costal groove along the inner inferior margin.
info.fact: The chest-drain triangle of safety sits just below it, at the fifth intercostal space in the mid-axillary line.

info.articulations: Bodies of T5 and T6 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T6 at its tubercle, and the sternal body through its own costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle, and costal groove; the shaft twists sharply at the angle.
info.fact: Rectus abdominis inserts on the costal cartilages of ribs five to seven, so this cartilage anchors the front of the abdominal wall.

info.articulations: Bodies of T6 and T7 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T7 at its tubercle, and the sternal body through its own costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, prominent angle, and costal groove on the inner inferior border.
info.fact: Usually the longest rib and the last true rib; its cartilage reaches the sternum near the xiphisternal joint.

info.articulations: Bodies of T7 and T8 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T8 at its tubercle, and indirectly the sternum via the seventh costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle, and costal groove carrying the intercostal bundle.
info.fact: The first false rib: its cartilage joins the rib above rather than the sternum, beginning the palpable costal margin.

info.articulations: Bodies of T8 and T9 by two facets on its head, the transverse process of T9 at its tubercle, and indirectly the sternum via the eighth costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Two-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle, and costal groove on the inner inferior surface.
info.fact: The transpyloric plane, at the L1 vertebral level, passes through the tips of the ninth costal cartilages.

info.articulations: Body of T10 by a single facet on its head, the transverse process of T10 at its tubercle, and indirectly the sternum via the ninth costal cartilage.
info.landmarks: Single-faceted head, neck, tubercle, angle, and a costal groove; the shaft is short and gently curved.
info.fact: The lowest rib to reach the costal margin; the subcostal plane, at the L3 level, crosses the inferior edge of its cartilage.

info.articulations: Body of T11 only, by a single facet on its head; it has no tubercle for a transverse process and its tip ends freely.
info.landmarks: Single-faceted head, no articular tubercle, a slight angle, a shallow costal groove, and a pointed cartilage-capped anterior tip.
info.fact: A floating rib whose free tip lies over the kidney, so the pleura and kidney are both at risk in posterior flank approaches.

info.articulations: Body of T12 only, by a single facet on its head; it has no tubercle, and its anterior end lies free in the abdominal muscles.
info.landmarks: Single-faceted head, no tubercle, no angle and no costal groove; a short tapering shaft with a free pointed tip.
info.fact: The shortest rib and the guide to the lumbar approach to the kidney; the pleural reflection crosses it, risking pneumothorax.

info.articulations: Both clavicles at the sternoclavicular joints and the costal cartilages of the first seven ribs on each side.
info.landmarks: Jugular notch, clavicular notches, manubrium, sternal angle of Louis, body, and the xiphoid process.
info.fact: The sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage, the T4/T5 disc, the tracheal bifurcation and both ends of the aortic arch.

info.articulations: The manubrium and first costal cartilage medially at the sternoclavicular joint, and the acromion of the scapula laterally at the acromioclavicular joint.
info.landmarks: Sternal end, acromial end, conoid tubercle and trapezoid line below the lateral third, and the subclavian groove for subclavius.
info.fact: The most commonly fractured long bone, usually at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds, and the first bone in the body to ossify.

info.articulations: The head of the humerus at the glenohumeral joint and the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.
info.landmarks: Glenoid cavity with supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles, spine, acromion, coracoid process, and the supraspinous, infraspinous and subscapular fossae.
info.fact: Injury to the long thoracic nerve paralyses serratus anterior and lets the medial border lift off the chest as a winged scapula.

info.articulations: The glenoid cavity of the scapula at the shoulder, the ulnar trochlear notch and the head of the radius at the elbow.
info.landmarks: Head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles with the intertubercular groove, deltoid tuberosity, radial groove, capitulum, trochlea and both epicondyles.
info.fact: The radial nerve hugs the radial groove, so a midshaft fracture classically produces wrist drop.

info.articulations: The capitulum of the humerus, the ulna at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, and the scaphoid and lunate at the wrist.
info.landmarks: Disc-shaped head, neck, radial tuberosity for biceps, interosseous border, dorsal tubercle of Lister, ulnar notch and styloid process.
info.fact: A Colles fracture breaks the distal radius after a fall on an outstretched hand, tipping the fragment dorsally into a dinner-fork deformity.

info.articulations: The trochlea of the humerus at the elbow and the radius at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints; an articular disc separates it from the carpus.
info.landmarks: Olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, ulnar tuberosity, head and styloid process.
info.fact: Olecranon and both epicondyles form a triangle when the elbow is flexed and a straight line when extended, a quick dislocation check.

info.articulations: The radius proximally, and the lunate, capitate, trapezium and trapezoid distally and medially.
info.landmarks: Proximal and distal poles, the narrow waist, and the palmar tubercle of the scaphoid.
info.fact: Its blood supply enters distally, so a waist fracture, tender in the anatomical snuffbox, can starve the proximal pole into avascular necrosis.

info.articulations: The radius proximally, scaphoid laterally, triquetrum medially, and the capitate and hamate distally.
info.landmarks: Crescent-shaped convex proximal surface, deeply concave distal surface for the capitate, and palmar and dorsal horns.
info.fact: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone; it slips forward into the carpal tunnel and compresses the median nerve.

info.articulations: The lunate laterally, the pisiform on its palmar surface, and the hamate distally; the articular disc separates it from the ulna.
info.landmarks: Pyramidal body, oval palmar facet for the pisiform, and the proximal facet that meets the triangular articular disc.
info.fact: It never touches the ulna directly; the triangular fibrocartilage of the articular disc always lies between them.

info.articulations: The triquetrum alone, by a single flat facet on its dorsal surface.
info.landmarks: Pea-shaped body with one flat dorsal facet, and the palmar attachments of flexor carpi ulnaris and the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments.
info.fact: A sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, it forms the medial wall of Guyon canal, where the ulnar nerve and artery run.

info.articulations: The scaphoid proximally, the trapezoid medially, and the first and second metacarpals distally.
info.landmarks: Saddle-shaped distal facet for the thumb, tubercle of the trapezium, and the groove for the flexor carpi radialis tendon.
info.fact: Its saddle joint with the first metacarpal lets the thumb oppose, and it is a classic site of thumb-base osteoarthritis.

info.articulations: The scaphoid proximally, the trapezium laterally, the capitate medially, and the second metacarpal distally.
info.landmarks: Wedge or boot shape with a broad dorsal and narrow palmar surface, and a saddle-shaped distal facet for the second metacarpal.
info.fact: The smallest bone of the distal carpal row and the least often fractured carpal, wedged tightly between its neighbours.

info.articulations: The scaphoid and lunate proximally, the trapezoid laterally, the hamate medially, and the second, third and fourth metacarpals distally.
info.landmarks: Rounded head, constricted neck, body, and the broad distal facet for the third metacarpal.
info.fact: The largest carpal bone and the keystone at the centre of the wrist; its name comes from caput, meaning head.

info.articulations: The lunate and triquetrum proximally, the capitate laterally, and the fourth and fifth metacarpals distally.
info.landmarks: Wedge-shaped body, the hook or hamulus projecting from the palmar surface, and two distal facets for the ulnar two metacarpals.
info.fact: The hook forms the lateral wall of Guyon canal; fracturing it on a club or racquet handle can injure the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

info.articulations: The trapezium at the saddle-shaped carpometacarpal joint and the proximal phalanx of the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Saddle-shaped base, short stout shaft, rounded head, and two sesamoid bones on the palmar side of the head.
info.fact: The shortest and stoutest metacarpal; a Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of its base.

info.articulations: The trapezoid mainly, plus the trapezium and capitate, the third metacarpal, and the proximal phalanx of the index finger.
info.landmarks: Deeply notched base gripping the trapezoid, long slender shaft, and a rounded head forming the index knuckle.
info.fact: The longest metacarpal; extensor carpi radialis longus inserts on the dorsal surface of its base.

info.articulations: The capitate proximally, the second and fourth metacarpals on either side, and the proximal phalanx of the middle finger.
info.landmarks: Base with a dorsolateral styloid process, shaft, and rounded head forming the most prominent knuckle.
info.fact: Extensor carpi radialis brevis inserts on its base, and its long axis is the midline about which fingers abduct and adduct.

info.articulations: The capitate and hamate proximally, the third and fifth metacarpals on either side, and the proximal phalanx of the ring finger.
info.landmarks: Small square base with two proximal facets, the slimmest shaft of the metacarpals, and a rounded head.
info.fact: Its mobile carpometacarpal joint, with the fifth, lets the ulnar side of the palm cup around an object during grip.

info.articulations: The hamate proximally, the fourth metacarpal laterally, and the proximal phalanx of the little finger distally.
info.landmarks: Base with a single hamate facet and a tubercle for extensor carpi ulnaris, shaft, and rounded head.
info.fact: The boxer fracture breaks its neck, driven by punching with a clenched fist, and the knuckle drops.

info.articulations: The head of the first metacarpal at the metacarpophalangeal joint and the distal phalanx of the thumb at the interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Concave oval base, palmar-flattened shaft, and a pulley-like trochlear head.
info.fact: Skier or gamekeeper thumb tears the ulnar collateral ligament running to its base, leaving the thumb unable to pinch firmly.

info.articulations: The proximal phalanx of the thumb alone, at the interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base, short broad shaft, and the distal tuberosity supporting the nail bed and pulp.
info.fact: The thumb has no middle phalanx, so it owns just one interphalangeal joint, flexed by flexor pollicis longus onto this base.

meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left index finger
Proximal phalanx of right index finger

info.articulations: The head of the second metacarpal at the metacarpophalangeal joint and the middle phalanx of the index finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Concave oval base for the metacarpal head, palmar-flattened shaft with ridges for the fibrous flexor sheath, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: The first dorsal interosseous inserts on the lateral side of its base and abducts the index finger away from the hand's midline.

meshNames: Middle phalanx of left index finger
Middle phalanx of right index finger

info.articulations: The proximal phalanx of the index finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint and its distal phalanx at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base with two shallow concavities, shaft bearing the flexor digitorum superficialis slips, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: The two slips of flexor digitorum superficialis insert on the sides of its shaft, which is what the standard FDS tendon test isolates.

meshNames: Distal phalanx of left index finger
Distal phalanx of right index finger

info.articulations: The middle phalanx of the index finger alone, at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base, short flattened shaft, and the distal tuberosity, the apical tuft that supports the nail bed and fingertip pulp.
info.fact: Mallet finger is avulsion of the terminal extensor tendon from its dorsal base, leaving the fingertip permanently drooped.

meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left middle finger
Proximal phalanx of right middle finger

info.articulations: The head of the third metacarpal at the metacarpophalangeal joint and the middle phalanx of the middle finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Concave oval base for the metacarpal head, palmar-flattened shaft with ridges for the fibrous flexor sheath, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: The longest proximal phalanx of the hand; because the middle finger is the axis of the hand, only dorsal interossei move it sideways.

meshNames: Middle phalanx of left middle finger
Middle phalanx of right middle finger

info.articulations: The proximal phalanx of the middle finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint and its distal phalanx at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base with two shallow concavities, shaft bearing the flexor digitorum superficialis slips, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: The longest middle phalanx; the central slip of the extensor tendon takes its dorsal base, and rupture gives a boutonniere deformity.

meshNames: Distal phalanx of left middle finger
Distal phalanx of right middle finger

info.articulations: The middle phalanx of the middle finger alone, at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base, short flattened shaft, and the distal tuberosity, the apical tuft that supports the nail bed and fingertip pulp.
info.fact: Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on its palmar base, the only tendon able to bend the distal interphalangeal joint.

meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left ring finger
Proximal phalanx of right ring finger

info.articulations: The head of the fourth metacarpal at the metacarpophalangeal joint and the middle phalanx of the ring finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Concave oval base for the metacarpal head, palmar-flattened shaft with ridges for the fibrous flexor sheath, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: The ring finger cannot extend independently: its extensor digitorum tendon is tethered to its neighbours by the juncturae tendinum.

meshNames: Middle phalanx of left ring finger
Middle phalanx of right ring finger

info.articulations: The proximal phalanx of the ring finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint and its distal phalanx at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base with two shallow concavities, shaft bearing the flexor digitorum superficialis slips, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: Flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the sides of its shaft, and the vincula carrying tendon blood supply attach on its palmar surface.

meshNames: Distal phalanx of left ring finger
Distal phalanx of right ring finger

info.articulations: The middle phalanx of the ring finger alone, at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base, short flattened shaft, and the distal tuberosity, the apical tuft that supports the nail bed and fingertip pulp.
info.fact: Jersey finger, avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus from its base, strikes the ring finger most often when a grip is torn open.

meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left little finger
Proximal phalanx of right little finger

info.articulations: The head of the fifth metacarpal at the metacarpophalangeal joint and the middle phalanx of the little finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Concave oval base for the metacarpal head, palmar-flattened shaft with ridges for the fibrous flexor sheath, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: Abductor digiti minimi, the hypothenar abductor, inserts on the medial side of its base.

meshNames: Middle phalanx of left little finger
Middle phalanx of right little finger

info.articulations: The proximal phalanx of the little finger at the proximal interphalangeal joint and its distal phalanx at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base with two shallow concavities, shaft bearing the flexor digitorum superficialis slips, and a trochlear head.
info.fact: The shortest middle phalanx, and the flexor digitorum superficialis slip to the little finger is often weak or absent.

meshNames: Distal phalanx of left little finger
Distal phalanx of right little finger

info.articulations: The middle phalanx of the little finger alone, at the distal interphalangeal joint.
info.landmarks: Base, short flattened shaft, and the distal tuberosity, the apical tuft that supports the nail bed and fingertip pulp.
info.fact: The smallest phalanx of the hand; its apical tuft anchors the nail bed, so a crush here usually splits the nail as well.

info.articulations: Femur at the acetabulum, the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint, and the opposite hip bone at the pubic symphysis.
info.landmarks: A fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis; note the acetabulum, obturator foramen, iliac crest and ischial tuberosity.
info.fact: The three parts fuse at the acetabulum during the teens, so a child's hip bone shows a Y-shaped triradiate cartilage.

info.articulations: Hip bone at the acetabulum, the tibia at the knee, and the patella in front; it never touches the fibula.
info.landmarks: Head with its fovea, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera, and the medial and lateral condyles.
info.fact: The longest and strongest bone in the body; its neck is the classic site of hip fracture in the elderly.

info.articulations: Only the femur, gliding on the patellar surface between the femoral condyles; it does not touch the tibia.
info.landmarks: Broad base above, pointed apex below, and posterior medial and lateral facets separated by a vertical ridge.
info.fact: The largest sesamoid bone, formed within the quadriceps tendon, where it lengthens the extensor lever arm at the knee.

info.articulations: Femur at the knee, the fibula at the proximal and distal tibiofibular joints, and the talus at the ankle.
info.landmarks: Medial and lateral condyles, intercondylar eminence, tibial tuberosity, sharp subcutaneous anterior border, and the medial malleolus.
info.fact: The tibia transmits essentially all body weight from knee to ankle, while the fibula carries almost none.

info.articulations: Tibia above and below at the tibiofibular joints, and the talus laterally through the lateral malleolus.
info.landmarks: Head with its apex, the neck, a slender shaft, and the lateral malleolus with its malleolar fossa.
info.fact: The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck, so a fracture there can cause foot drop.

info.articulations: Talus above at the subtalar joint and the cuboid in front at the calcaneocuboid joint.
info.landmarks: Calcaneal tuberosity, sustentaculum tali, the fibular (peroneal) trochlea, and the groove for flexor hallucis longus.
info.fact: The largest tarsal and the heel bone; a fall from height can drive the talus down into it.

info.articulations: Tibia and fibula above at the ankle, the calcaneus below, and the navicular in front.
info.landmarks: Head, neck and body, with the trochlea above plus lateral and posterior processes grooved for flexor hallucis longus.
info.fact: No muscle or tendon attaches to the talus, and its retrograde blood supply risks avascular necrosis after a neck fracture.

info.articulations: Talus behind, the three cuneiforms in front, and sometimes the cuboid laterally.
info.landmarks: Concave posterior facet for the talar head, three anterior cuneiform facets, and the prominent navicular tuberosity medially.
info.fact: Named for its boat shape; tibialis posterior attaches mainly to its tuberosity, a palpable landmark on the medial foot.

info.articulations: Calcaneus behind, the fourth and fifth metatarsals in front, the lateral cuneiform medially, and sometimes the navicular.
info.landmarks: Cuboid tuberosity and, on the plantar surface, the distinctive groove for the fibularis longus tendon.
info.fact: The most lateral tarsal; the fibularis longus tendon hooks under it to cross the sole toward the first metatarsal.

info.articulations: Navicular behind, the first metatarsal in front, the intermediate cuneiform laterally, and the base of the second metatarsal.
info.landmarks: Wedge shape with its broad base plantar, a kidney-shaped anterior facet, and the tibialis anterior insertion medially.
info.fact: The largest cuneiform; tibialis anterior and fibularis longus attach to opposite sides of it, balancing the forefoot.

info.articulations: Navicular behind, the second metatarsal in front, and the medial and lateral cuneiforms on either side.
info.landmarks: Wedge shape with its broad base facing dorsally, a small anterior facet, and flanking medial and lateral facets.
info.fact: The smallest cuneiform; the three are named medial, intermediate and lateral counting outward from the great toe.

info.articulations: Navicular behind, third metatarsal in front, intermediate cuneiform and cuboid at its sides, plus the second and fourth metatarsal bases.
info.landmarks: Wedge shape with its base dorsal, an anterior facet for the third metatarsal, and a lateral facet for the cuboid.
info.fact: The only cuneiform that touches the cuboid; with the medial cuneiform it forms the mortise gripping the second metatarsal base.

info.articulations: Medial cuneiform at its base and the proximal phalanx of the great toe at its head.
info.landmarks: Base with a kidney-shaped cuneiform facet, a short thick shaft, and a head grooved below for two sesamoids.
info.fact: The shortest and stoutest metatarsal; the sesamoids beneath its head take much of the load at push-off.

info.articulations: All three cuneiforms at its recessed base, the first and third metatarsals at its sides, and its proximal phalanx.
info.landmarks: Base wedged between the cuneiforms, the longest shaft of the metatarsals, and a rounded head.
info.fact: Its recessed base makes it the most rigid metatarsal and the usual site of the march (stress) fracture.

info.articulations: Lateral cuneiform at its base, the second and fourth metatarsals at its sides, and its proximal phalanx in front.
info.landmarks: Base with facets for the lateral cuneiform and neighbouring metatarsals, a slender shaft, and a rounded head.
info.fact: The middle of the five; metatarsals two to four look alike, so count from the great toe.

info.articulations: Cuboid at its base, the lateral cuneiform medially, the third and fifth metatarsals beside it, and its proximal phalanx.
info.landmarks: Base carrying both cuboid and cuneiform facets, a slender shaft, and a rounded head.
info.fact: It straddles the cuboid and the lateral cuneiform, marking where the lateral column of the foot begins.

info.articulations: Cuboid at its base, the fourth metatarsal medially, and the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe.
info.landmarks: Prominent tuberosity (styloid process) on the lateral base for fibularis brevis, plus the shaft and head.
info.fact: Inversion injury can avulse that tuberosity; a fracture just distal to it is the Jones fracture.

synonyms: proximal phalanx of digit 1 of foot
meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left big toe
Proximal phalanx of right big toe

info.articulations: First metatarsal at its base and the distal phalanx of the great toe at its head.
info.landmarks: Concave oval base, a short stout shaft, and a trochlear head; flexor hallucis brevis attaches at the base.
info.fact: The largest phalanx in the foot, and the great toe has only two phalanges, so no middle one exists.

synonyms: distal phalanx of digit 1 of foot
meshNames: Distal phalanx of left big toe
Distal phalanx of right big toe

info.articulations: Only the proximal phalanx of the great toe, at its base.
info.landmarks: Base, a very short shaft, and a flattened distal tuberosity supporting the nail bed.
info.fact: Flexor hallucis longus inserts on its base, giving the great toe its powerful push-off at the end of stance.

synonyms: proximal phalanx of digit 2 of foot
meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left second toe
Proximal phalanx of right second toe

info.articulations: Second metatarsal at its base and the middle phalanx of the second toe at its head.
info.landmarks: Concave base, a slender shaft, and a trochlear head, with the extensor expansion spread over its dorsal surface.
info.fact: The second toe is often the longest; when it outreaches the great toe this is called Morton's toe.

synonyms: middle phalanx of digit 2 of foot
meshNames: Middle phalanx of left second toe
Middle phalanx of right second toe

info.articulations: Proximal phalanx behind and the distal phalanx of the second toe in front.
info.landmarks: Broad base with two concave facets, a very short shaft, and a small trochlear head.
info.fact: Flexor digitorum brevis inserts here after splitting to let flexor digitorum longus pass through to the distal phalanx.

synonyms: distal phalanx of digit 2 of foot
meshNames: Distal phalanx of left second toe
Distal phalanx of right second toe

info.articulations: Only the middle phalanx of the second toe, at its base.
info.landmarks: Base, a tiny shaft, and a distal tuberosity that broadens to support the nail.
info.fact: Flexor digitorum longus inserts on its base; the lesser distal phalanges are the smallest bones of the foot.

synonyms: proximal phalanx of digit 3 of foot
meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left third toe
Proximal phalanx of right third toe

info.articulations: Third metatarsal at its base and the middle phalanx of the third toe at its head.
info.landmarks: Concave base, slender shaft, and trochlear head, with lumbricals and interossei attaching near the base.
info.fact: Persistent extension here with flexion further along the toe produces the hammer toe deformity seen with tight shoes.

synonyms: middle phalanx of digit 3 of foot
meshNames: Middle phalanx of left third toe
Middle phalanx of right third toe

info.articulations: Proximal phalanx behind and the distal phalanx of the third toe in front.
info.landmarks: Broad base with paired concave facets, a short shaft, and a small trochlear head.
info.fact: Middle phalanges exist only in toes two to five, the quickest way to rule out the great toe.

synonyms: distal phalanx of digit 3 of foot
meshNames: Distal phalanx of left third toe
Distal phalanx of right third toe

info.articulations: Only the middle phalanx of the third toe, at its base.
info.landmarks: Base, a very short shaft, and a flattened tuberosity lying under the nail.
info.fact: Distal phalanges are recognised by that spade-like tuberosity, which anchors the fleshy pulp and the nail bed.

synonyms: proximal phalanx of digit 4 of foot
meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left fourth toe
Proximal phalanx of right fourth toe

info.articulations: Fourth metatarsal at its base and the middle phalanx of the fourth toe at its head.
info.landmarks: Concave base, slender shaft, and trochlear head, with the plantar plate and extensor expansion attached around it.
info.fact: Proximal phalanges are the longest of the three rows, so a long slim toe bone is proximal.

synonyms: middle phalanx of digit 4 of foot
meshNames: Middle phalanx of left fourth toe
Middle phalanx of right fourth toe

info.articulations: Proximal phalanx behind and the distal phalanx of the fourth toe in front.
info.landmarks: Broad base with two facets, a stubby shaft, and a small trochlear head.
info.fact: Lesser middle phalanges are so short they are mistaken for distal ones until you look for the tuberosity.

synonyms: distal phalanx of digit 4 of foot
meshNames: Distal phalanx of left fourth toe
Distal phalanx of right fourth toe

info.articulations: Only the middle phalanx of the fourth toe, at its base.
info.landmarks: Base, barely any shaft, and a small distal tuberosity beneath the nail.
info.fact: Fractures of a lesser toe like this are usually managed by taping it to the neighbouring toe.

synonyms: proximal phalanx of digit 5 of foot
meshNames: Proximal phalanx of left little toe
Proximal phalanx of right little toe

info.articulations: Fifth metatarsal at its base and the middle phalanx of the fifth toe at its head.
info.landmarks: Concave base, short shaft, and trochlear head, with flexor digiti minimi brevis attaching at the base.
info.fact: This is the bone that takes the hit when a little toe catches the furniture, the classic stubbed toe.

synonyms: middle phalanx of digit 5 of foot
meshNames: Middle phalanx of left little toe
Middle phalanx of right little toe

info.articulations: Proximal phalanx behind and, when it stays separate, the distal phalanx of the fifth toe in front.
info.landmarks: Small base, almost no shaft, and a tiny head; it is often fused with the distal phalanx.
info.fact: In many people the little toe's middle and distal phalanges fuse, leaving that toe with only two bones.

synonyms: distal phalanx of digit 5 of foot
meshNames: Distal phalanx of left little toe
Distal phalanx of right little toe

info.articulations: Only the middle phalanx of the fifth toe, at its base, when the two have not fused.
info.landmarks: Base, minimal shaft, and a small tuberosity supporting the nail.
info.fact: The smallest bone in the foot, and commonly fused to the middle phalanx of the little toe.
